rule.description: LangChain tool description is too short to guide model selection
rule.full_description: A description under 40 characters is rarely enough to convey what a tool does, what it returns, and when to call it rather than a similarly named neighbor. LangChain passes this text to the model as the tool's only selection signal, so a stub like "Gets data." leaves scope and preconditions to guesswork. In an AgentExecutor loop the cost compounds: each mis-selected call consumes an iteration against LC-102's max_iterations budget, so a run can exhaust its steps re-trying tools it picked badly and return nothing useful.
rule.help: Expand the description to at least a full sentence covering inputs, outputs, and the situation in which this tool should be used over the alternatives.

rule.description: LangChain tool has no description
rule.full_description: LangChain exposes a tool to the model through its description: for an @tool-decorated function or a StructuredTool, the description defaults to the wrapped function's docstring. A tool with no docstring (and no explicit description=) reaches the model as a bare name, so the model cannot tell what the tool does or when to call it — it will skip the tool or invoke it with the wrong arguments. This is the single highest-leverage authoring fix.
rule.help: Add a one-paragraph docstring to the wrapped function describing what the tool does, the inputs it expects, and what it returns — or pass an explicit description= to StructuredTool/Tool. The model reads this string verbatim.

A tool with no docstring (and no explicit description=) reaches the model as a bare name, so the model cannot tell what the tool does or when to call it — it will skip the tool or invoke it with the wrong arguments. This is the single highest-leverage authoring fix.

rule.description: certifi bundles emSign root CAs with compromised intermediate CA keys
rule.name: LanguageSpecificPackageVulnerability
rule.full_description:
Certifi versions before 2026.10.18 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root certificate in their bundled CA store. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to this root have compromised private keys and the CA has revoked them. 

An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname. If the attacker is also on-path, they can intercept or modify TLS traffic from clients that trust the certifi bundle. Examples include `requests`, `urllib3` and `pip`, and the Python.org macOS installer.

Certifi 2026.10.18 removed all emSign roots from the bundle. Certifi 2026.10.19 restored the emSign roots that are not affected. Upgrade to 2026.10.19 or later, and rebuild container images that vendor certifi.

rule.description: aiohttp: aiohttp: Host-Only cookie protection bypass via untrusted subdomain
rule.name: LanguageSpecificPackageVulnerability
rule.full_description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.4, Host-Only scope on an existing parent-domain cookie can be removed by a subdomain. A user who accesses an untrusted subdomain can consequently have host-only protections stripped from cookies, although impact is limited when applications do not reflect those cookies to a browser. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

rule.description: aiohttp: aiohttp: Security control bypass via request scheme spoofing
rule.name: LanguageSpecificPackageVulnerability
rule.full_description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.4, an attacker can send an absolute-form request that causes Request.scheme to use attacker-controlled request-target scheme data instead of the connection protocol. Applications that use Request.scheme for security decisions can consequently be tricked into treating an unencrypted connection as encrypted or an encrypted connection as unencrypted. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

rule.description: Ambiguous LangChain tool name
rule.full_description: The tool name is a generic verb that says nothing about what the tool acts on. The name sits directly beside the description in what the model sees, so it is half the selection signal, and a name like process or handle spends that half on nothing — the model either calls the tool for the wrong job or passes over it entirely. A LangChain agent is routinely handed a dozen or more tools at once, so a name that does not discriminate competes against every neighbor in the list, and each wrong pick spends an iteration against LC-102's max_iterations budget.
rule.help: Rename to a verb-object form that names the thing acted on: summarize_invoice, refund_charge, fetch_order_status. Keep the description for the detail and let the name carry the subject.

In an AgentExecutor loop the cost compounds: each mis-selected call consumes an iteration against LC-102's max_iterations budget, so a run can exhaust its steps re-trying tools it picked badly and return nothing useful.

rule.description: LangChain tool raises without a structured error contract
rule.full_description: This tool raises an exception it never catches. LangChain does not feed tool exceptions back to the model unless you opt in: with the default handle_tool_error=False the exception propagates out of the AgentExecutor and aborts the run, so the model is never told the step failed and the caller gets a traceback instead of an answer. Opting in with handle_tool_error=True is barely better — the model receives the raw str(exception), an opaque sentence with no failure mode, no indication whether a retry could succeed, and whatever internal detail the message happened to carry (file paths, hostnames, query fragments).
rule.help: Catch the failure modes you expect and return a structured result the model can branch on — an error field naming the failure and a retryable flag — instead of letting the exception escape. Where you do want LangChain to intercept, set handle_tool_error to a callable that maps the exception to a specific, model-readable message rather than to True.

rule.description: 'RUN cd ...' to change directory
rule.name: Misconfiguration
rule.full_description: Use WORKDIR instead of proliferating instructions like 'RUN cd … && do-something', which are hard to read, troubleshoot, and maintain.

Use WORKDIR instead of proliferating instructions like 'RUN cd … && do-something', which are hard to read, troubleshoot, and maintain.
